domain: Cultural Anthropology / Technology Adoption / Behavioral Economics
topic_summary: Analysis of the hypothesis that widespread fork adoption in Europe altered bite configuration and contributed to the reduction of edge-to-edge bite (overbite development), representing a case of structural change through technology-mediated behavioral drift rather than conscious selection. The fork case tests whether path-naturalization can occur without identifiable beneficiaries when an alternative simply becomes unavailable through disuse.

key_entities: Fork (eating utensil technology, 11th-17th century European diffusion)
Overbite/dental occlusion (vertical overlap of upper over lower incisors)
Table manners code (civilizing process behavioral norms)
Knife-based eating (pre-fork alternative requiring anterior tooth engagement)
key_tensions: Fork-mediated vs anterior-tooth-mediated food processing (mechanical path selection)
Conscious etiquette adoption vs unconscious biomechanical consequence (intentionality)
key_mechanisms: Anterior tooth disengagement (fork eliminates need for incisor tearing/holding)
Developmental plasticity (juvenile jaw development responds to loading patterns)
Technology-behavior-morphology feedback (tool use → behavior → skeletal adaptation)
key_absences: Beneficiary of overbite emergence (no actor gained advantage from the shift)
Selection pressure favoring overbite (no fitness or social reward)
Counter-technology preserving edge-to-edge bite (no fork-alternative maintenance path)
